questions.title: How do you define non-functional requirements?
questions.quick: I make them measurable. Instead of saying the system must be fast, I agree response-time percentiles under a defined workload. Instead of high availability, I agree an availability target plus recovery time and recovery point objectives. I also capture concurrent users, data volumes, security needs, audit retention, backup frequency and monitoring expectations. I get business owners to confirm the targets and their cost, because NFRs drive architecture choices and become the basis for acceptance and load testing.
questions.revision: Turn vague qualities into measurable targets with a workload and a test: latency percentiles, availability, RTO, RPO, volumes, retention. NFRs drive architecture and acceptance testing.
questions.detailed:
**Non-functional requirements (NFRs)** describe *how well* a system must behave rather than *what* it does. They are often the biggest drivers of architecture, and the most commonly left vague. The rule is: **every NFR needs a number, a condition and a way to verify it.**

## From vague to measurable

| Vague statement | Measurable version |
|---|---|
| "Must be fast" | 95th percentile of the search API under 500 ms with 300 concurrent users and a 10 million record dataset |
| "Highly available" | 99.9% monthly availability for the core workflow, measured at the load balancer |
| "Must not lose data" | RPO of 5 minutes, RTO of 1 hour |
| "Secure" | Single sign-on, role-based access, encryption in transit and at rest, penetration test before launch |
| "Auditable" | All changes to approvals retained for seven years, tamper-evident |

(The figures above are illustrative; real values come from the business.)

## Categories to cover

- Performance and capacity: latency, throughput, concurrency, data growth.
- Availability and recovery: uptime target, RTO, RPO, backup frequency.
- Security and compliance: authentication, authorisation, data classification, audit.
- Scalability and elasticity.
- Operability: logging, monitoring, alerting, deployment frequency.
- Usability, accessibility and browser or device support.
- Maintainability and testability.

## How to elicit them

Ask "what happens if this is unavailable for an hour?", "how many users at the busiest moment?" and "what would a breach cost?". Show the cost of each target, since each additional level of availability or latency raises cost.

## Common mistakes

- Copying a generic list without business input.
- Targets without a workload definition, making them untestable.
- Setting every NFR to the maximum, producing an unaffordable design.
- Treating NFRs as late-stage testing instead of design inputs.

**Example (hypothetical):** a field-service app states "sync completes within 30 seconds on a poor mobile network for up to 200 queued records". That single NFR justifies batching, compression and an offline-first design.
followUps: How do you verify a latency NFR before release?
What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
What if the business insists on 100% availability?
How do NFRs conflict with each other, for example security and performance?

questions.title: What is an Architecture Decision Record?
questions.quick: An Architecture Decision Record is a short document capturing one significant architecture decision: the context, the decision, the alternatives considered, the rationale, the consequences and the risks. An example would be why we chose a modular monolith over microservices for the first release. I keep them in the repository next to the code, so decisions stay traceable. They reduce repeated debates when people or requirements change, and they show when a decision should be revisited.
questions.revision: An ADR is a short, versioned record of one significant decision: context, options, choice, rationale and consequences. It makes decisions traceable and stops the same debate repeating.
questions.detailed:
An **Architecture Decision Record (ADR)** is a short, dated document describing a single architecturally significant decision and why it was made. The value is not the paperwork but the preserved reasoning.

{{diagram:adr}}

## Typical structure

```markdown
# ADR-012: Use a modular monolith for the first release

Status: Accepted (supersedes none)
Context: Team of six, domain boundaries still evolving,
         limited operations capacity, 9-month deadline.
Decision: One deployable with enforced module boundaries.
Options considered: microservices from day one; third-party suite.
Consequences: simple operations and local transactions;
         scaling is per-application until a module is extracted.
Risks and revisit trigger: reporting load; review after pilot.
```

## What deserves an ADR

Choices that are costly to reverse or affect many teams: architecture style, database technology, messaging approach, identity provider, major vendor integration, multi-tenancy model. Routine implementation choices do not need one.

## Practices that work

- Store ADRs as Markdown in the repository, numbered and reviewed through pull requests.
- Keep them to about a page; record *alternatives rejected and why*.
- Never edit history. When a decision changes, write a new ADR and mark the old one as superseded.
- Record the trade-offs honestly, including the downsides you accepted.

## Common mistakes

- Writing ADRs after the fact with no real alternatives.
- Treating them as approval gates that slow every change.
- Burying them in a wiki nobody finds.
- Recording the decision but not the context, which makes it unintelligible a year later.

**Example (hypothetical):** a new engineer asks why events are published through an outbox table instead of publishing directly. The ADR explains the dual-write failure risk that motivated it, saving a long discussion.

diagrams.title: ADR lifecycle
diagrams.alt: A decision need leads to a proposed ADR, which is reviewed and then accepted; later it may be superseded by a new ADR that links back to it.

followUps: Which decisions do you think are worth an ADR?
How do you handle a decision that turns out to be wrong?
How do ADRs fit with an architecture review board?
Where do you store them and who approves them?

questions.title: How do you avoid overengineering?
questions.quick: I separate mandatory requirements from speculative future ones. I design for the known non-functional requirements and the evolution points we can reasonably predict, and I avoid abstractions, services or infrastructure without a clear need. I prefer a small, well-structured MVP with explicit extension points and revisit the design when evidence changes. I count complexity as development effort, operational burden, failure modes and total cost of ownership, not just lines of code.
questions.revision: Build for known requirements and likely change points, not imagined ones. Judge complexity by effort, operations, failure modes and total cost; keep extension points and revisit with evidence.
questions.detailed:
**Overengineering is adding complexity that the current and near-term requirements do not need.** It is costly because complexity has a recurring price: more code to maintain, more to operate, more ways to fail and more to explain to new people.

## Practical guardrails

1. **Tie every component to a requirement.** If you cannot name the NFR or business need that justifies a queue, a cache, a new service or an abstraction layer, defer it.
2. **Design for known change, not hypothetical change.** Isolate parts that are *likely* to change (such as a third-party integration) behind an interface. Do not generalise everything.
3. **Prefer reversible decisions.** Choose the simple option when it can be replaced later at a modest cost, and invest design effort in the hard-to-reverse choices (data model, identity, tenancy).
4. **Start small, with explicit seams.** A modular monolith with clear boundaries leaves room to grow.
5. **Use evidence.** Load tests, production metrics and incident history justify adding caching, partitioning or services.
6. **Count the whole cost.**

| Cost dimension | Question to ask |
|---|---|
| Build | How much extra development and testing is this? |
| Operate | Who monitors, patches and is on call for it? |
| Failure | What new ways can this break? |
| Cognitive | Can a new team member understand it quickly? |
| Ownership | What is the total cost over several years? |

## The opposite risk

Underengineering is real too: ignoring security, auditability, data integrity or recovery because "it is just an MVP". The aim is *right-sized*, driven by NFRs that were agreed explicitly.

## Common mistakes

- Building a generic configurable framework before a second use case exists.
- Adopting a fashionable technology without a team that can operate it.
- Splitting into services "for scalability" with no measured need.

**Example (hypothetical):** a team plans an event-streaming platform for a workflow with a few hundred events per day. A relational table plus a background worker meets the need, with a documented trigger (volume or consumer count) for revisiting the decision.
followUps: How do you tell a justified abstraction from a speculative one?
How do you push back when stakeholders ask for features "for the future"?
Can you give an example of underengineering and its consequences?
How do ADRs help here?

questions.title: How do you modernize a legacy application?
questions.quick: I would first assess business criticality, dependencies, the data model, performance, security and operational risk. Before major changes I establish tests and observability so I can see regressions. Then I prioritise by business value and modernise incrementally: refactoring, introducing API boundaries and using the strangler pattern where suitable. I avoid a full rewrite unless there is a compelling reason and a credible migration plan. Every phase needs compatibility, rollback and data-integrity safeguards.
questions.revision: Assess, add tests and observability, then modernise incrementally by value using API seams and the strangler pattern. Avoid big-bang rewrites; every step needs rollback and data safeguards.
questions.detailed:
**Modernisation means improving a legacy system's maintainability, security, performance or capabilities while the business keeps running.** The central risk is disrupting something critical, so the default is incremental change.

## Approach

1. **Assess.** Map business criticality, users, integrations, data stores, technology age, security exposure, performance issues and who still understands it. Note what hurts: slow releases, outages, unsupported platforms, cost.
2. **Create a safety net.** Add characterisation tests (tests that capture current behaviour), monitoring, logging and a reliable build and deploy pipeline. Without these you cannot tell whether a change broke anything.
3. **Pick a strategy per component.** Common options:

| Option | Meaning | When it fits |
|---|---|---|
| Retain | Leave it alone | Stable, low-value, low-risk |
| Rehost | Move infrastructure as is | Need to exit a data centre quickly |
| Refactor | Improve code and structure in place | Sound design, poor code |
| Re-platform | Update runtime or database with few changes | Unsupported platform |
| Strangle and replace | Replace capability by capability | Large system needing continuous operation |
| Rewrite | Rebuild | Only with strong justification |
| Retire | Switch off | Functionality no longer needed |

4. **Sequence by value and risk.** Start with a well-bounded, valuable capability to prove the approach.
5. **Introduce seams.** Wrap the legacy system with APIs so new components integrate through stable contracts, using an anti-corruption layer to keep the old model from leaking.
6. **Protect data.** Plan migration, dual-running and reconciliation, with verified backups and rollback.
7. **Decommission** old parts once traffic has moved and results are verified.

## Common mistakes

- A full rewrite that takes years, while the legacy system keeps changing, so the target never catches up.
- Modernising technology without fixing the underlying design problems.
- Neglecting data migration until the end.
- No clear success measures such as deployment frequency or defect rate.

**Example (hypothetical):** a decade-old inspection system is wrapped by an API gateway, and a new mobile-friendly inspection module replaces one workflow first while all other features keep running in the old system.
followUps: When is a full rewrite actually justified?
How do you test a system with no tests before changing it?
How do you migrate data without downtime?
How do you get stakeholder buy-in for a multi-year modernization?

questions.title: What is the strangler pattern?
questions.quick: The strangler pattern replaces a legacy system gradually. I put a routing layer in front, send selected functionality to new components and let everything else keep running in the old system. As each slice proves stable, I move more traffic across until the legacy parts can be retired. It reduces the risk of a big-bang migration because each step is small and reversible. A good first candidate is a bounded capability, such as reporting or a single workflow.
questions.revision: Put a facade in front of the legacy system and route capability by capability to new components until the old system can be switched off. Small, reversible steps instead of big-bang.
questions.detailed:
The **strangler fig pattern** (named after a vine that gradually surrounds a tree) incrementally replaces a legacy system with a new one. At every moment there is a working system.

{{diagram:strangler}}

## Steps

1. **Insert a facade** (reverse proxy, API gateway or routing layer) in front of the legacy system. Initially it forwards everything unchanged.
2. **Choose a slice.** Pick a bounded capability with clear inputs and outputs and meaningful value.
3. **Build the new component** and run it alongside the old one. Consider shadow traffic or comparison of results before cutover.
4. **Route** that capability to the new component, using a feature flag or percentage rollout so you can switch back immediately.
5. **Handle data.** Decide who owns the data for the slice. Options include synchronising through events or change data capture, or migrating the data and making the new component the owner. Plan reconciliation.
6. **Repeat**, then remove the dead legacy code and finally the facade if no longer needed.

## Trade-offs

| Advantage | Drawback |
|---|---|
| Continuous delivery of value | Temporary complexity: two systems and a router |
| Small, reversible risk | Data synchronisation is the hardest part |
| Learning from early slices | Needs discipline to finish and decommission |

## Common mistakes

- Choosing slices that cut across tightly coupled data, forcing constant synchronisation.
- Never retiring the old code, leaving permanent double maintenance.
- Letting the legacy data model leak into the new design. Use an anti-corruption layer.
- No verification of parity between old and new behaviour.

**Example (hypothetical):** an old procurement application is fronted by a gateway. The "supplier onboarding" screens are rebuilt first and routed to a new service for ten per cent of users, then all users. Purchase orders stay in the legacy system until their own migration.

diagrams.title: Strangler pattern routing
diagrams.alt: Clients call a routing facade; requests for migrated capabilities go to new services while all other requests continue to the legacy system; both can use data synchronisation.

followUps: How do you keep data consistent while both systems are live?
Which capability would you migrate first and why?
How do you verify the new component behaves the same as the old?
What is an anti-corruption layer?

questions.title: How would you design a multi-tenant SaaS platform?
questions.quick: I would start by defining isolation, compliance and cost requirements per tenant. A shared application with a shared database and a tenant identifier on each record is the most cost-effective, if tenant identity is enforced consistently in authorization and data access. Stronger isolation comes from schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant. I would add centralized tenant resolution, tenant-scoped authorization, quotas, per-tenant backup and restore plans, and automated isolation tests. Isolation must be enforced on the server, never by frontend filters.
questions.revision: Pick the tenancy model from isolation, compliance and cost needs: shared tables, schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant. Resolve tenant centrally and enforce it server-side, with quotas and tests.
questions.detailed:
A **multi-tenant** platform serves many customers (tenants) from shared infrastructure while keeping their data and experience separate. The design question is *how much to share*, balancing cost, isolation, operability and compliance. (Security controls and leakage reviews are covered separately in the security-governance question on securing a multi-tenant platform.)

{{diagram:tenancy}}

## Isolation models

| Model | Description | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pooled (shared tables) | One schema, a tenant identifier on every row | Cheapest, simplest to operate and onboard | Isolation depends on every query; noisy neighbours; per-tenant restore is hard |
| Schema per tenant | One database, separate schema each | Better logical separation, easier per-tenant export | Migrations run per schema; limits at large tenant counts |
| Database per tenant | Separate database (or instance) | Strongest isolation, per-tenant restore and tuning | Highest cost and operational overhead |

Hybrid models are common: pooled for most tenants, dedicated databases for tenants with strict compliance or heavy load.

## Cross-cutting design

- **Tenant resolution:** derive the tenant once, centrally, from a trusted source such as the authenticated token, subdomain or tenant claim, and carry it in request context.
- **Tenant-scoped data access:** a shared repository layer or database row-level security applies the tenant condition automatically instead of relying on each developer.
- **Configuration and customisation** per tenant (features, branding, workflows) without code forks.
- **Noisy-neighbour control:** quotas, rate limits and fair queueing for background jobs.
- **Lifecycle:** onboarding automation, backup and restore, data export and tenant offboarding.
- **Observability:** logs and metrics tagged by tenant.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing the model once and assuming it can never change. Keep data access abstracted to allow migration of large tenants.
- Relying on UI filters or optional `WHERE tenant_id` clauses.
- Global caches or job queues keyed without tenant.
- Schema migrations that cannot be rolled out across hundreds of tenants safely.

**Example (hypothetical):** a facilities SaaS runs most customers pooled, and offers a dedicated database to a regulated customer that requires it, using the same codebase.

diagrams.title: Tenant isolation models
diagrams.alt: Three models from lowest to highest isolation: shared database with a tenant id column, one schema per tenant in a shared database, and a separate database per tenant. All sit behind one shared application tier with tenant resolution.

followUps: How would you migrate a growing tenant from pooled to dedicated storage?
How do you handle schema migrations across thousands of tenants?
How do you prevent one tenant from degrading others?
How would you price and package isolation tiers?
